articles.description: Vetster review built only from Vetster's own pages: Vetster Plus at $12/month billed annually, a single appointment from $102 one-time, the VetsterRx fee table and the prescribing rules, every figure with its official source, checked 2026-09-26.
articles.h1: Vetster review: what Vetster's own pages say about price, appointments and prescriptions
articles.lede: Quick answer: Vetster is a marketplace where you book a licensed veterinarian for a video appointment, 24/7. On its own published numbers there are two ways to pay - Vetster Plus at $12/month billed annually, which includes 4 same-day video appointments a year, or a single appointment starting at $102 one-time. Both options include 48-hour follow-up live messaging with your vet and prescriptions through VetsterRx. Prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision and depends on your state's rules, and Vetster states online vets are not a replacement for emergency clinics. Every figure below was read from vetster.com on 2026-09-26.

faqs.a: Vetster Plus is $12/month, billed annually. Twelve months at that published price comes to $144 (12 x $12, arithmetic on Vetster's own figure) and it includes 4 same-day video appointments a year plus unlimited messaging with registered vet techs. A single appointment starts at $102 one-time at marketplace rates. Products, pharmacy fees and shipping are charged separately.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Vetster Plus and paying per appointment?
faqs.a: Vetster Plus is a yearly subscription: 4 same-day video appointments a year, 50% off additional bookings, up to 2 unused appointments carried over, unlimited messaging with registered vet techs, all pets under one plan. Paying per appointment buys one visit for one pet at marketplace rates, starting at $102 one-time, with the 48-hour follow-up messaging included.

faqs.q: Can a Vetster vet prescribe medication?
faqs.a: Yes, when a valid vet-client-patient relationship is in place and the condition can be handled safely over video. Whether that relationship can be established online depends on your state's rules, federal guidance often expects a real exam first, and prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision. The prescription is then sent to the pharmacy you choose - Vetster is not a pharmacy.

faqs.q: What are Vetster's pharmacy and shipping fees?
faqs.a: Pharmacy fee per order: $7 for Vetster Plus members, $14 for non-members. Compounding fee per medication: $10 for members, $20 for non-members. Standard shipping (2-3 business days) is free for members and for non-member orders over $45; express shipping (1-2 business days) is $19 for everyone.

faqs.q: Is Vetster available in my state?
faqs.a: Both payment options are listed as available in all states, and VetsterRx fulfillment is listed as available in all 50 States. Whether a vet can prescribe during an online visit still depends on your state's rules, so that is confirmed during the appointment itself.

faqs.q: When should I not use an online vet?
faqs.a: Go in person immediately for difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapse or seizures, severe or sudden pain, suspected poisoning, major trauma, or being unable to urinate. Vetster states online vets are not a replacement for emergency clinics and that an online vet will direct you to appropriate in-person care.

faqs.q: How long can I message my vet after the appointment?
faqs.a: 48-hour follow-up live messaging with your vet is included in both payment options. Vetster Plus separately includes unlimited messaging with registered vet techs for help with pet health, behaviour, nutrition and urgent advice.

faqs.q: What does this Vetster review check, and what does it not check?
faqs.a: It checks only what Vetster publishes on its own pages - the subscription price, the single-appointment price, the VetsterRx fee table, the prescribing rules and the emergency list - each with its source link and check date of 2026-09-26. It does not test-drive appointments, and it does not repeat prices from third-party comparison sites.

articles.disclaimer: Editorial review of Vetster's own published pages - not veterinary advice and not a paid endorsement. Prices, inclusions and fees change, so every figure carries its official source link and a check date of 2026-09-26; re-read the official page before you pay. Nothing here is a diagnosis: in an emergency, go to a clinic.

blocks.html:
There is no independent score for an online vet service, and we will not invent one. This Vetster review reads only Vetster's own pages: the Vetster Plus page (price, inclusions, billing and cancellation FAQ), the VetsterRx pharmacy page (the full fee table) and Vetster's two wellness guides (how virtual care works, and how prescriptions work). Every number in the table below carries a link to the page it was read from and a check date.

Where Vetster does not publish something - for example, what a single appointment costs beyond the printed starting price, or how long a subscription has been running for a given pet - this page says not published on the official page instead of guessing.

blocks.h2: Vetster Plus vs a single appointment - published figures only
What the numbers say side by side
blocks.html:
The subscription and the single visit are priced on different units, so compare the units first. Vetster prints $12/month and then states in its own FAQ that billing occurs annually, once per year. A single appointment is printed as a one-time starting price of $102 and billed at whatever the chosen veterinarian's marketplace rate is - that is why the table says starting at and not costs.

The fee table is where the two options quietly diverge. The same pharmacy page prints both rates side by side: $7 vs $14 per order, $10 vs $20 per compounding, free standard shipping vs free only above $45. Express shipping is $19 either way.

Vetster is explicit about the boundary, and a review that hides it would be useless. Its own guide says to seek immediate in-person or emergency care for seven signs: difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapse or seizures, severe or sudden pain, suspected poisoning, major trauma, and being unable to urinate. Its preparation guide repeats the point in different words - telehealth is not a substitute for emergency care.

Prescribing sits in the middle. Vetster's prescription guide says a valid vet-client-patient relationship is required in almost every state, that the open question is whether that relationship can be built over video, that federal guidance often expects a real exam first, and that prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision. Practical consequence for a reviewer: the appointment can end with "your pet needs to be seen in person", and that is the clinic standard, not a runaround.

articles.h1: Online vet vs in-person vet: when a video visit is enough and when you must go to a clinic
articles.lede: Quick answer: book an online vet for quick answers, after-hours questions, follow-up care, chronic-condition management, preventive care and medication questions. Go in person immediately - before any video call - if your pet has difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapses or seizes, has severe or sudden pain, suspected poisoning, major trauma, or is unable to urinate. Those seven signs are Vetster's own list, read from its online vet guide on 2026-09-26. A prescription is a separate question: it needs a valid vet-client-patient relationship, and whether that can be built over video depends on your state's rules.

faqs.a: Yes. Vetster states that online vets are licensed veterinarians who have completed accredited veterinary training, and that they complete the same education and licensing process as all veterinarians.

faqs.q: When should I use an online vet instead of going in person?
faqs.a: For quick answers when something has changed with your pet, after hours when physical clinics are closed, follow-up care, chronic condition management, preventive recommendations, medication questions and quality-of-life discussions - plus the everyday clusters Vetster lists: skin, ear and eye concerns, digestive and urinary changes, behaviour, mobility and ongoing care.

faqs.q: When should I go straight to a clinic or emergency hospital?
faqs.a: Immediately, if your pet has difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapses or seizes, shows severe or sudden pain, is suspected of poisoning, has suffered major trauma, or is unable to urinate. Vetster also states plainly that telehealth is not a substitute for emergency care.

faqs.q: Can an online vet prescribe medication?
faqs.a: Only when a valid vet-client-patient relationship is in place and the condition is appropriate for virtual care. Whether that relationship can be built over video depends on state rules, federal guidance often expects a real exam first, and prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision. The prescription then goes to the pharmacy you choose.

faqs.q: What can an online vet not do?
faqs.a: They cannot perform a hands-on exam, and Vetster's own guidance puts conditions needing lab work or imaging, complex or serious illnesses, medications requiring close monitoring, higher-risk drugs and many controlled substances on the in-person side of the line.

faqs.q: Do I need my pet on camera during the appointment?
faqs.a: Yes, for as much of the appointment as possible. Vetster explains that the vet relies on what they can see on screen, that having your pet present creates the basis for the veterinary-client-patient relationship, and that without your pet on screen the vet may be unable to diagnose or prescribe.

faqs.q: Is there such a thing as a free online vet?
faqs.a: General pet information is widely available for free, but Vetster states that personalized care from a licensed veterinarian is typically a paid service, because licensed veterinarians are legally responsible for the care they provide.

articles.disclaimer: This page restates only Vetster's own published guidance - it is not veterinary advice and not a diagnosis. Checked 2026-09-26, source links attached to every line; re-read the official pages before you act. In an emergency, go to a clinic.

blocks.html:
The online vet vs in-person question is usually answered with opinions. This page answers it with one brand's published rules: Vetster runs both a telemedicine marketplace and a preparation guide written by its editorial team and verified by its own veterinarians, and it publishes exactly when it sends people to a clinic instead. Both columns below come from those pages - nothing is filled in from forums or comparison sites.

One honest limitation: the right-hand column is thinner than the left, because Vetster publishes its own side of the story and does not publish clinic prices or clinic opening hours. Those cells say not published on the official Vetster pages checked for this row rather than borrowing a number from somewhere else.

blocks.h2: Online vet vs in-person - the conditions side by side

blocks.html:
Run the urgent list first, everything else second. Vetster's seven emergency signs come before any other consideration, and its preparation guide repeats the principle: many people use virtual care precisely to find out whether their pet needs in-person or emergency care.

Then split by what the vet can actually do through a screen. Symptoms, history, photos, movement on camera, medication questions and follow-ups travel well over video. Lab work, imaging, a hands-on exam and higher-risk prescribing do not - and Vetster's own two-column table draws that line for you.

blocks.h2: The prescription question, which is where the confusion lives
blocks.html:
Three separate layers decide whether you leave an online visit with medication. First the relationship: almost every state requires a valid vet-client-patient relationship before any vet can prescribe, and Vetster says the open question is whether that relationship can be established over video. Second the federal picture: for many prescription medications, federal guidance expects the relationship to rest on a real exam or visit. Third the judgment: Vetster's guide says prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision, and a vet may still ask for a hands-on exam, lab work or imaging first.

If the prescription does happen, the pharmacy is your choice - Vetster states it is not a pharmacy and sends the script directly to the local or online pharmacy you pick, with the service fee shown as a labelled line item before checkout.
